en: Their thoughts turned toward progress,
And the times encountered prosperity.
They scattered his ashes to the sky,
And extinguished the scattered brands.
From this world they cleansed away
The infidel entirely.
Their great desire was fulfilled,
And death came to the great villain.
Goodness entered the world;
The incurable sickness that had struck,
The myriad arrows lodged in their ribs,
Was healed and subsided.
Resentful brows relaxed,
Their wretched anguish abated,
And their moon-bright faces cleared.
The people clamored and held a feast;
The wicked swine was gone,
And order among the people was restored.
Sarybai had waged war
For many months and many years,
And they had suffered, held in misery.
On that day the multitude,
From the dire and savage affliction,
Through the support of Seytek
And the heroism of Kuyaly,
Were delivered from Sarybai.
The people settled down in peace,
Lying at ease upon their well-fed flanks.
They migrated freely to mountain pastures,
And settled upon the foothills.
They lived according to their will,
Hunting deer whenever they grew bored.
When the multitude was not weary,
They played freely together,
Rode young horses and flew hunting birds,
Marked out the ordo field and cast their knucklebones,
And won surpassing honor.
Amid grand and lively festivities,
They raced horses and young steeds,
Along the banks of broad Talas.
On the banks of broad Talas,
Below Tört-Kül,
In the garden once planted
By the gray wolf Prince Manas,
The son inherited from his father
The throne upon which he sat,
And his palace was of gold.
When they saw Aichürök,
At the edge of the open steppe,
Near the seer’s dark cave,
Before the golden throne,
The people swarmed like teeming worms
And gathered together.
Some wore wound turbans,
And prayed, crying, “My God!”
They had full, ripened grain
And herds of all four kinds.
They wore mottled robes,
And did not roam about wrestling.
They crowded in from every side,
Their blue felt caps trampled underfoot.
From their encampments their livestock covered the green,
And the people came in mounted companies.
People of every kind arrived.
The reason the people came was this:
Sarybai had been consigned to the fire,
And the long-suffering people
Were delivered on that day.
Their moonlike faces brightened,
Their pounding hearts grew calm,
And true contentment filled them;
Their faces truly brightened.
The stored and guarded treasury,
To every one of the people,
Because fierce Sarybai was dead,
They scattered without withholding a thing.
Dead fires were kindled anew,
The dying returned to life,
The severed were joined,
And the scattered were gathered.
Burning hearts grew calm,
Furrowed brows relaxed,
Their painful ailments subsided,
And the people’s spirits rose.
Multitudes of every kind arrived,
Many coming from every tribe.
They devised wonders beyond imagining,
As though surpassing the moonlit world.
The great feast they held then
Seemed to cover the face of the earth.
They heaped up glowing red embers,
And the encamped people voiced their grievances.
Those who knew and those who had seen
Heard it from long-eared elders;
From all these countless people,
A great assembly formed,
And the uproar split the sky.
Dust flew into the heavens
As the people gathered in throngs.
It became a most joyous feast,
And the grateful people could not rejoice enough.
“When Sarybai held us captive,
Unable to stir from one place,
We endured six or seven months;
We suffered exceedingly,
All because of Sarybai,” they said.
From Sarybai’s venom
Red-tailed riding camels died,
And the finest red-necked champions,
Souls whose like could not be found, died.
He fought to possess this Talas;
Many men and many lions
He drove away, estranged from their people.
He extinguished the burning fire
And carried off the plunder in one night;
Thus he brought the people to ruin.
He made mankind grieve,
Made every back stoop,
And made dear eyes bulge with anguish.
He savaged the courageous
And tore at them without sparing a soul.
The cur took them as plunder
And uprooted the settled folk.
He spread strife and turmoil through the world
And left souls burning in his wake.
At the slightest blink he took a life,
Sarybai, shaped like a wild boar.
Upon hero Kuyaly and Seytek
Descended the people’s fortune and blessing.
The torment inflicted by Sarybai
Became a mark of infamy carved in stone.
The madman burned in the fire;
The ruin he had brought upon the people
Had become a pestilent sickness,
Oppressing many people,
A cruel and grievous affliction
Against which all the heroes assembled.
Some souls were crazed and leaderless,
Wanderers with no one to pursue them,
Torn apart without a chief.
Those who always resisted,
Standing upon their honor,
Were slaughtered to the last.
That gnawing sorrow subsided.
“O Almighty, restore to me
My land he ravaged,” they prayed.
They held a feast without stint,
Spending all they possessed.
Baitailak, son of Bakai,
Thus began speaking to the people,
Softly beginning his weighty words.
The son whose name was renowned
Conceived an unfathomable plan
And held a feast beyond all measure.
When he said, “Hear these words of mine,”
The multitude blessed by Kyzýr
Thickened together like curdled yogurt.
“Baitailak’s wisdom
Is manifest and exemplary;
What he says is right,” they said.
When all their livestock and wealth
Were lavishly scattered,
And the finest words were spoken,
No pleasure was left unfulfilled.
Men grappled on horseback for the kök-börü,
Until their poles bent,
And heroic warriors jousted.
The victors threw down their rivals,
And mocked one another;
The fallen were left empty-handed,
While the victors claimed the prize.
It became an unimaginable spectacle,
An immense feast:
“The feast of hero Seytek,” they said,
“The design of Kuyaly and the people,” they said,
“For they saved our lives from torment.
It is the feast of our lion,” they said.
They bared the great camels’ teeth,
Let their lower lips droop,
Made their two humps tower,
And their necks arch like ducks,
Their shaggy manes trailing.
All the multitude
They made shout aloud with joy.
They slaughtered bright-red riding camels
And mares with fat a span thick.
They slaughtered equally from all four kinds,
And laid out wealth in equal measure.
They slaughtered livestock of all four kinds
And raised a mountain of meat like Ala-Too.
They meant to gather
Every person upon the earth.
They made the dew seem a swelling lake;
The people gathered and joined their strength,
Assembling the entire nation without exception.
The air steamed with meat and fat,
The people rejoiced and the land overflowed.
“It is dear Seytek’s feast,” they said,
“He whose back is like the lofty Ala-Too,
For he defeated Sarybai,” they said.
There on the banks of Talas,
At the feast of hero Seytek,
The Russians ate their fill and departed,
Saying, “If this Seytek lives,
The eighteen thousand worlds
Will marvel at him.”
The Chinese ate their fill and departed,
Saying, “If this Seytek lives,
Upon every crooked mortal
He will bring destruction.”
For nine days they had
The treasury doors thrown open.
To orphans, the poor, and widows,
To paupers who owned no livestock,
They scattered wealth lavishly.
His generosity was revealed;
To the hungry and destitute,
To the weak and impoverished,
Without valuing wealth by so much as a hair,
They measured it out with a whip,
And ordered it given to them.
They set the people’s hearts at ease
And made rich all who had lacked.
They had Kushkun and Durkun sing,
And thus delighted the people.
Their hearts surged with joy,
And many among the people reveled.
Each solitary soul became as a thousand,
And each presence shone like the Night of Power.
“Father Seytek, hero Seytek,
May he be the bulwark of the people,”
Many among the people blessed him.
“We escaped certain slaughter,
We were spared an open grave;
From the wretch who ruled in our fathers’ day,
We escaped his wrath,” they said.
The people’s hearts had been oppressed;
“Let the people proclaim his glory,” they said,
And the people’s hearts were stirred.
They appealed to Khan Seytek,
As though now destined to see wonders,
And pronounced their blessing,
As though he would allot each one an inheritance.
Spoken words cannot describe their dignity;
Among the people giving blessings
There were saints and every kind of soul.
Among those pronouncing blessings,
Some wore white turbans large as cauldrons,
And when they cried out, their voices rang like the call to prayer.
Seated, they were broad as hearths;
Their mouths seemed thick as forearms,
And their haunches broad as an embrace.
They were masters of royal encampments,
Khans of many different kinds.
Crying “Allah!” they raised their hands
And turned their faces toward the qibla.
